blocks.text: A 15-year-old girl has never had a period. Every month for the last six months she has had cramping lower abdominal pain lasting several days, and today you notice a bluish bulge at the introitus. A simple structural problem is the cause, and a good history and examination reveal it before any blood test. This unit teaches the order of thinking: history, examination, classification, and then targeted investigation.

blocks.markdown:
**The gynaecological history.** Begin with the presenting complaint in the woman's own words, then ask systematically:

- **Menstrual history**: age at menarche, date of last menstrual period (LMP), cycle length (first day of one period to first day of the next), duration and heaviness of bleeding (clots, flooding, soaking through protection, impact on daily life), intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding, pain and premenstrual symptoms.
- **Sexual and contraceptive history**, pregnancy possibility, and sexually transmitted infection risk.
- **Cervical screening** history, obstetric history, previous surgery.
- **Medical, drug and family history**, including bleeding disorders, thyroid disease, anticoagulants, hormones and antipsychotics.
- **Systemic and lifestyle**: weight change, exercise, stress, eating disorder, hirsutism, galactorrhoea, headache and visual symptoms.

**Normal cycle** in the adult is roughly 24 to 38 days, with bleeding lasting up to about 8 days, and variation between cycles of up to about 9 days. Regular cycles with premenstrual symptoms such as breast tenderness and mood change usually indicate ovulation.

**Examination.** Explain the procedure, obtain consent, offer a chaperone and allow the woman to stop at any time. Assess the **general** state (BMI, pallor, hirsutism, acne, thyroid, signs of Turner syndrome or virilisation), the **abdomen** (masses, tenderness), then the **pelvis**: inspect the vulva, use a **speculum** to see the vagina and cervix (discharge, polyps, lesions; take swabs or cervical screening if due), and perform a **bimanual examination** to assess uterine size, position, mobility and tenderness, adnexal masses or tenderness, and cervical motion tenderness. Examination is not always needed (for example in a young girl or an adolescent not sexually active); abdominal ultrasound may suffice.

blocks.title: Heavy menstrual bleeding and the PALM-COEIN system
blocks.text: Heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB) is excessive menstrual blood loss that interferes with a woman's physical, social, emotional or material quality of life. The FIGO classification of abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) by cause uses PALM-COEIN. Structural causes (PALM): Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma (fibroid), Malignancy and hyperplasia. Non-structural causes (COEIN): Coagulopathy, Ovulatory dysfunction, Endometrial disorder, Iatrogenic, Not yet classified.

rows: Heavy, painful periods, bulky tender uterus
Heavy regular periods, pressure symptoms, enlarged irregular uterus
Age over 45, obesity, persistent irregular bleeding
Heavy bleeding since menarche, bruising, epistaxis
FBC, ferritin, coagulation screen, von Willebrand testing
Irregular cycles, PCOS, thyroid disease, perimenopause
Regular heavy bleeding with normal examination and scan
blocks.caption: Mapping PALM-COEIN to clinical clues and tests.

blocks.markdown: **Investigating heavy bleeding.** Exclude pregnancy where relevant. Check a full blood count and consider ferritin. Test for a coagulation disorder (coagulation screen, von Willebrand factor studies) if heavy bleeding has been present since menarche or there are bleeding symptoms. Offer ultrasound if there are symptoms or examination findings suggesting a structural cause or if first-line treatment fails. **Endometrial sampling** is considered with persistent intermenstrual bleeding, age 45 or older with treatment failure, or risk factors for endometrial hyperplasia such as obesity and polycystic ovary syndrome. First-line medical treatment options for HMB without structural pathology include the levonorgestrel intrauterine system, tranexamic acid, NSAIDs and combined hormonal contraception (check NICE NG88).

blocks.title: Classifying abnormal bleeding in a perimenopausal woman
blocks.prompt: A 47-year-old woman with BMI 38 has had irregular cycles of 20 to 60 days with episodes of very heavy bleeding for 8 months. Examination: uterus normal size, mobile, non-tender. Pregnancy test negative, haemoglobin 98 g/L. Classify the likely cause and outline the investigations.

steps.text: Pattern: irregular and unpredictable cycles suggest ovulatory dysfunction (O). Anovulation causes unopposed oestrogen stimulation of the endometrium, producing irregular and sometimes heavy bleeding. Perimenopause and obesity both favour this.

Exclude structural and malignant causes: age 47 with obesity and persistent irregular bleeding is a risk profile for endometrial hyperplasia or cancer (M). Arrange transvaginal ultrasound and endometrial sampling or hysteroscopy.
Complete the work-up: haemoglobin of 98 g/L signals anaemia, so check ferritin and treat iron deficiency; consider thyroid function. Normal uterus on examination makes a large fibroid less likely.

blocks.answer: Probable ovulatory dysfunction (with endometrial malignancy or hyperplasia to be excluded); investigate with pregnancy test, FBC and ferritin, ultrasound and endometrial sampling.

blocks.markdown:
**Amenorrhoea.** **Primary amenorrhoea** is the failure to menstruate by age 15 with normal secondary sexual characteristics, or by age 13 with no breast development (definitions vary slightly between guidelines). **Secondary amenorrhoea** is cessation of periods for 3 months in a woman with previously regular cycles (6 months if previously irregular). **Pregnancy is the commonest cause of secondary amenorrhoea**, so a pregnancy test comes first.

Use anatomy and the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis as a framework:

- **Outflow tract**: imperforate hymen, transverse vaginal septum (cyclical pain, normal development), Asherman syndrome (intrauterine adhesions after instrumentation or infection; secondary amenorrhoea).
- **Uterus or vagina absent**: Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser (MRKH) syndrome (46,XX, normal breasts and pubic hair, absent uterus) versus **androgen insensitivity syndrome** (46,XY, normal breasts, scant or absent pubic and axillary hair, blind-ending vagina, testes).
- **Ovary**: Turner syndrome (45,X; short stature, webbed neck, streak ovaries), premature ovarian insufficiency (loss of ovarian function before age 40), polycystic ovary syndrome. Low oestrogen with **high FSH** points to ovarian failure.
- **Hypothalamus and pituitary**: functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea (low weight, excessive exercise, stress; low or normal FSH and LH with low oestradiol), hyperprolactinaemia (prolactinoma, drugs such as antipsychotics and metoclopramide), thyroid disease, pituitary lesions.

blocks.title: Interpreting hormone results in secondary amenorrhoea
blocks.prompt: A 28-year-old has had no periods for 7 months. She has hot flushes. Pregnancy test negative, prolactin and TSH normal. FSH is 58 IU/L and oestradiol is low, confirmed on a repeat sample 4 weeks later. Interpret the result.

steps.text: Exclude common reversible causes first: pregnancy is negative, prolactin and TSH are normal, so hyperprolactinaemia and thyroid disease are excluded.

Interpret the axis: a high FSH with low oestradiol means the pituitary is responding appropriately to lack of ovarian feedback, so the problem lies in the ovary. Vasomotor symptoms at age 28 confirm hypo-oestrogenism.

Diagnosis: premature ovarian insufficiency (persistent raised FSH on two samples at least 4 weeks apart, thresholds vary by guideline). Next steps: karyotype, fragile X premutation testing and autoimmune screen, bone health and cardiovascular counselling, and hormone replacement until about the age of natural menopause.

blocks.answer: Premature ovarian insufficiency (hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism); investigate cause and offer hormone replacement for symptoms and long-term bone and cardiovascular protection.

items: Exclude pregnancy in any woman of reproductive age with amenorrhoea or abnormal bleeding.
In primary amenorrhoea, check growth, breast development, pubic hair and the uterus and vagina by examination or ultrasound.
Measure FSH, LH, oestradiol, prolactin, TSH and consider testosterone; a high FSH means ovarian failure; a low or normal FSH means the hypothalamus or pituitary.
Obtain karyotype in primary amenorrhoea with high FSH or suspected disorders of sex development.
Review drugs, weight, exercise, eating disorder and stress.

blocks.title: Look for the structural answer first
blocks.text: In primary amenorrhoea with normal breast development and cyclical pain, think outflow obstruction; with normal breasts, absent uterus and normal pubic hair, think MRKH; with scant pubic hair, think androgen insensitivity. Examination and ultrasound narrow the differential before the karyotype confirms it.

points: A structured menstrual, sexual and medical history with consented, chaperoned examination (speculum and bimanual) guides investigation.
AUB is classified using PALM-COEIN into structural and non-structural causes; investigation depends on age, risk and pattern.

Primary and secondary amenorrhoea are investigated using pregnancy testing, hormone profiles (FSH, oestradiol, prolactin, TSH), imaging and karyotype, organised by site: outflow, ovary or hypothalamic-pituitary axis.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes good practice before a speculum and bimanual examination?

options.text: Explain the examination, gain consent, offer a chaperone and allow the woman to stop at any time
Proceed without explanation to avoid causing anxiety
Examine only after the woman has been given sedation
Perform the examination in every woman, including girls who have never been sexually active

questions.correctOptionText: Explain the examination, gain consent, offer a chaperone and allow the woman to stop at any time

distractorRationale.a: Correct: informed consent, a chaperone offer and the right to stop are core professional standards.
distractorRationale.b: Lack of explanation removes informed consent.
distractorRationale.c: Sedation is not routine and complicates consent.
distractorRationale.d: Examination is not always necessary; ultrasound may suffice in some situations.

questions.explanation: Pelvic examination is intimate and requires explicit consent, privacy and a chaperone offer. It should be performed only when it will change management.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman has cycles every 29 days with breast tenderness and mood change a few days before each period. What does this history most suggest about her cycles?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: regular cycles with premenstrual symptoms usually indicate ovulation and progesterone exposure.
distractorRationale.b: Anovulatory cycles are typically irregular and unpredictable.
distractorRationale.c: Premature ovarian insufficiency causes oligomenorrhoea or amenorrhoea.
distractorRationale.d: Hyperprolactinaemia suppresses ovulation and causes irregular or absent cycles.

questions.explanation: Regular cycle length with predictable premenstrual symptoms reflects the luteal phase and progesterone production, indicating ovulation. Anovulatory bleeding is irregular because it lacks the cyclic progesterone withdrawal.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old has regular heavy periods with pelvic pressure and urinary frequency. Bimanual examination reveals a firm, irregularly enlarged uterus of about 14 weeks' size. According to the PALM-COEIN classification, which category is most likely?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a firm, irregularly enlarged uterus with pressure symptoms suggests fibroids.
distractorRationale.b: Coagulopathy causes heavy bleeding but does not enlarge the uterus.
distractorRationale.c: Ovulatory dysfunction causes irregular bleeding and a normal-sized uterus.
distractorRationale.d: Iatrogenic bleeding relates to drugs or devices; no such history is given.

questions.explanation: Regular heavy cycles indicate ovulation, so the cause is more likely structural or haemostatic. A firm, irregularly enlarged uterus with pressure on the bladder points to leiomyomas, which are confirmed by pelvic ultrasound.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old has had heavy periods since menarche at 12. She has frequent nosebleeds and bruises easily, and her mother has had heavy periods too. Which diagnosis should be investigated first?

options.text: An inherited bleeding disorder such as von Willebrand disease

questions.correctOptionText: An inherited bleeding disorder such as von Willebrand disease

distractorRationale.a: Correct: heavy bleeding since menarche with mucosal bleeding and family history suggests an inherited bleeding disorder.
distractorRationale.b: Endometrial cancer is rare at 15 and does not explain nosebleeds.
distractorRationale.c: Premature ovarian insufficiency causes amenorrhoea, not heavy bleeding.
distractorRationale.d: A polyp does not cause easy bruising or nosebleeds.

questions.explanation: Heavy bleeding from menarche with epistaxis, easy bruising and a family history is typical of a coagulopathy. Investigation includes FBC, ferritin, a coagulation screen and von Willebrand factor studies, with haematology referral.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old student presents with 5 months of secondary amenorrhoea. She is 1.58 m tall and weighs 41 kg, and she runs daily. Calculate her body mass index in kg/m^2.
questions.explanation: BMI = weight divided by height squared = 41 / (1.58 x 1.58) = 41 / 2.4964 = 16.4 kg/m^2. This is well below the usual underweight threshold of 18.5, and with excessive exercise it points to functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea once pregnancy and other causes are excluded.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old has primary amenorrhoea. She is 143 cm tall with a webbed neck and no breast development. FSH is markedly raised and oestradiol is low. Which investigation will confirm the most likely diagnosis?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: karyotype 45,X (or mosaic) confirms Turner syndrome.
distractorRationale.b: Hyperprolactinaemia does not explain short stature, webbed neck and a high FSH.
distractorRationale.c: A pituitary lesion would give low or normal gonadotrophins.
distractorRationale.d: Hysteroscopy assesses the uterine cavity, not the cause of ovarian failure.

questions.explanation: Short stature, a webbed neck and absent puberty with high FSH and low oestradiol indicate streak ovaries from Turner syndrome. Karyotyping confirms the diagnosis, which also requires screening for cardiac and renal anomalies.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old has primary amenorrhoea with normal breast development, absent pubic and axillary hair, and a blind-ending vagina. Pelvic ultrasound shows no uterus. Which diagnosis is most likely?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: absent pubic and axillary hair with normal breasts and no uterus indicates complete androgen insensitivity.
distractorRationale.b: MRKH has normal pubic hair because androgen action is normal.
distractorRationale.c: An imperforate hymen has a normal uterus, with cyclical pain and a bulging membrane.
distractorRationale.d: Turner syndrome presents with short stature and absent breast development.

questions.explanation: In complete androgen insensitivity the 46,XY gonads produce testosterone, but receptors do not respond, so there is no pubic hair; testicular anti-Mullerian hormone prevents a uterus from forming, while peripheral conversion of androgen to oestrogen gives breast development. MRKH differs by having normal pubic hair and a 46,XX karyotype.

questions.stem: True or false: in a woman of reproductive age with new secondary amenorrhoea, a pregnancy test is the first investigation.
questions.explanation: Pregnancy is the most common cause of secondary amenorrhoea and must be excluded before hormone assays or imaging. Doing so avoids unnecessary or unsafe investigation.

questions.stem: Outline how abnormal uterine bleeding is classified by cause using PALM-COEIN, giving a clinical clue for each of three categories, and explain when endometrial sampling is indicated.
markingGuide: Structural PALM: polyp, adenomyosis, leiomyoma, malignancy and hyperplasia
Non-structural COEIN: coagulopathy, ovulatory dysfunction, endometrial, iatrogenic, not yet classified
At least three correct clinical clues, for example fibroid with enlarged irregular uterus, coagulopathy with bleeding since menarche, ovulatory dysfunction with irregular cycles
Endometrial sampling indicated for persistent intermenstrual bleeding, age 45 or over with treatment failure, or risk factors such as obesity and PCOS
Pelvic ultrasound used for structural causes; full blood count and ferritin for anaemia
questions.explanation: PALM-COEIN separates structural lesions that can be seen on imaging or histology from functional and systemic causes, which directs investigation. Endometrial sampling is targeted at women with risk for hyperplasia or cancer, not all women with heavy bleeding.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old has 8 months of secondary amenorrhoea, intermittent milky nipple discharge and frontal headaches. Pregnancy test is negative. Outline your history, examination and investigations and the likely diagnosis.
markingGuide: History: drug history (antipsychotics, metoclopramide, antidepressants), visual symptoms, weight change, thyroid symptoms, contraceptive use
Examination: visual fields (bitemporal hemianopia), breast examination for galactorrhoea, BMI, thyroid, signs of hypo-oestrogenism
Investigations: serum prolactin (repeat; consider macroprolactin), TSH, FSH, LH, oestradiol
MRI of the pituitary if prolactin persistently raised
Likely diagnosis: hyperprolactinaemia, for example prolactinoma, which suppresses GnRH pulsatility and hence ovulation
Treatment: dopamine agonist for prolactinoma; stop or change culprit drugs
questions.explanation: Raised prolactin inhibits hypothalamic GnRH pulses, lowering LH and FSH and so suppressing ovulation and periods, and can cause galactorrhoea. A mass effect from a macroadenoma explains the headaches and visual-field defects, so imaging and visual fields are essential.
